idea.title: Paper Towel Roll Letter Hunt
idea.summary: Children roll, look through and talk about the paper towel tube while the educator names letters and sounds. Toddlers can post the foam letters through a tube made into a simple chute, and the infant explores the cardboard tube textures with close adult support.
setup: Check the paper towel roll for sharp edges and tape any rough spots smooth. Keep the foam letters in a shallow tray or basket near the group.
Lay a sheet of yellow construction paper on the floor or table as a rug for the group to sit around.
Using the black marker, write the first letter of each child's name on a separate paint stick, but use only letters the group already knows, and keep the paint sticks out of mouths.
Put the pipe cleaners and crayons in a small bin where everyone can reach them.
Sit on the floor with the group and keep the infant on a soft cushion in front of you.

tiers.label: Tube Explorers
steps: Hold the paper towel roll near the infant so they can touch it, mouth it safely and feel the cardboard texture.
Roll the tube gently across the infant's hands and say the sound of a letter they can see, like 'mmm' for M.
Hold one large foam letter up to the infant's face, say its name, and let them reach for it.
Watch the infant look through the tube at your face, then say 'hello' through the tube.
tiers.stretch: Let the infant hold the tube with both hands while you guide their wrists to move it up and down.

tiers.label: Letter Chute
steps: Show the toddler how to stand the paper towel roll upright on the paper.
Ask each toddler to find a foam letter, name it, and drop it through the tube, then say the letter sound out loud.
Help toddlers gather pipe cleaners and bend them into simple shapes, then slide the shape through the tube and say what it looks like.
Let toddlers scribble a line with a chunky crayon on yellow paper while you sing the alphabet song together.
tiers.stretch: Ask toddlers to find a letter that starts like their own first name and drop it down the chute.

tiers.label: Letter Chute
steps: Show the children how to stand the paper towel roll upright and drop a foam letter through it.
Ask children to name the letter before it goes through, then say a word that starts with its sound.
Invite them to bend pipe cleaners into a letter shape, then pass it through the tube and guess the letter together.
Let them write or draw one thing they found on the yellow paper.
tiers.stretch: Ask children to hide a letter inside the tube and have a friend guess which one it is by its sound.

tiers.label: Letter Chute
steps: Set up the tube and ask school-age children to take turns dropping letters through and reading the word they make with a partner.
Have children write a short word on a paint stick with the black marker, then trade it with a friend to read aloud.
Invite them to shape pipe cleaners into a letter and explain which sound it makes.
tiers.stretch: Challenge children to write three words that start with the same letter and sort them on the yellow paper.

safety: Keep all foam letters and pipe cleaners away from infants and toddlers when no adult is close, since small pieces can come loose.
Remove any loose tape or torn paper edges from the paper towel roll before each use.
Keep the plastic bag out of reach, and never use it in this activity.
Always keep the infant within arm's reach of an adult during the activity.
An educator supervises the whole time.
Check the space and every material before you start.
watch_for: Notice which letters each child recognizes and which sounds they try out loud.
Note how toddlers use the tube, whether they drop, look through it or try to fit things inside.
Record how the infant responds to textures and voices.
talk: What sound does this letter make, and what other word starts with it?
Where else in the room could we find a tube like this?
What do you think is inside the tube when you look through it?
idea.home_idea: Roll up a paper towel tube and hunt for letters or objects that start with the same sound as the child's name, then talk about them together.
